query: Which material can be used for ductility, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Adding oxygen as an interstitial dopant to a Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi high-entropy alloy will improve its ductility compared to the undoped or nitrogen‐doped variant by promoting the formation of ordered oxygen complexes that favor a more deformation‐tolerant microstructure.
generation.material_initial_state: A Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi high-entropy alloy produced by arc-melting, forming a primarily disordered, solid-solution BCC structure with baseline ductility (elongation around 10–12%).
generation.intervention: Introduce oxygen via the addition of TiO2 during alloy processing to form (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98O2 (O-2 HEA).
generation.conditions: Process under high-purity argon atmosphere with multiple remeltings and drop casting, followed by room-temperature tensile testing.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of ordered interstitial oxygen complexes that modify local atomic arrangements and reduce the continuity of brittle phases.
generation.mechanism: Interstitial oxygen forms ordered complexes that alter the lattice distortion and interfere with the formation of a continuous brittle phase, thereby enhancing dislocation mobility and improving ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in ductility (observed as higher tensile elongation up to ~20%) with a moderate yield strength improvement, relative to the base alloy or a nitrogen-doped variant.
generation.baseline: The base Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi HEA without oxygen exhibits lower ductility (elongation near 10–12%) and yield strength in the range of ~810–1362 MPa, depending on processing.
generation.boundary: The increased ductility is expected at room temperature under standard tensile testing; however, the exact degree of improvement may depend on oxygen concentration, processing uniformity, and potential trade-offs with damping performance.
generation.uncertainty: While the oxygen-doped HEA is predicted to be more ductile, the precise quantitative improvement and its interaction with other mechanical properties (e.g., yield strength and damping) remain to be fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi HEAs using identical arc-melting and casting procedures: one set doped with oxygen (via TiO2) to form the O-2 variant, and a control set (or alternatively, a nitrogen-doped variant using TiN). Conduct room-temperature tensile tests on specimens from both sets. Use X-ray diffraction (XRD), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), or atom probe tomography (APT) to verify the formation and distribution of ordered interstitial complexes. Compare the tensile elongation and yield strength between the groups.
measurements: Phase composition and microstructural analysis via XRD/TEM/APT
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxygen-doped HEA does not show a statistically significant increase in tensile elongation (e.g., moving from ~10–12% to ~20% ductility) relative to the control or nitrogen-doped HEA under identical conditions, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

Question: How can the room temperature ductility of an initially brittle refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) with a continuous ordered B2 matrix be improved while maintaining high yield strength?. System: Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr (RHEA). Processing: Condition (1): Cast, hot isostatically pressed (HIPed) at 1200 °C for 2 h, homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h, slow cooled at 10 °C/min. Condition (2): Condition (1) solutionized at 1400 °C for 20 min, water quenched. Condition (3): Condition (2) annealed at 600 °C for 120 hrs, water quenched.. Test conditions: Room temperature (25 °C) and elevated temperature (600 °C) uniaxial compression tests at an initial strain rate of 0.001 s⁻¹.. Findings: Condition (1) exhibited a continuous ordered B2 matrix with discrete BCC precipitates, resulting in a yield strength of 2032 MPa but only 4.7% compressive fracture strain.; Condition (2) formed a single-phase weakly ordered BCC structure with nanometer-scale B2 regions, achieving >60% compressive ductility but a lower yield strength of 1065 MPa.; Condition (3) achieved an 'inverted' microstructure with a continuous disordered BCC matrix and discrete ~50 nm B2 precipitates, yielding 1345

Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy alloys be designed to simultaneously achieve high Snoek-type damping capacity, high mechanical strength, and high ductility at elevated temperatures?. System: Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi base HEA, (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98O2 (O-2 HEA), and (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98N2 (N-2 HEA). Processing: Arc-melting of pure metals (purity >99.9 wt%), TiN (99.9 wt%), and TiO2 (99.9 wt%) in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere; remelted at least eight times; drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold (10 mm × 10 mm × 60 mm). Test conditions: Damping measured via multifunction internal friction apparatus at 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0 Hz, temperature range 300–1100 K, heating rate 2 K min⁻¹, max strain amplitude 2 × 10⁻⁴; Tensile tests at room temperature, strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Findings: The O-2 HEA achieved a peak damping capacity (tanδ_max) of 0.020 at 1.0 Hz, while the N-2 HEA reached 0.027 at 1.0 Hz.; The N-2 HEA exhibited a yield strength of 1362 MPa and elongation of ~11.9%, while the O-2 HEA showed 1138 MPa yield strength and ~20% elongation.; The peak damping temperature (T_p) for the HEAs was approximately 730–747 K at 1.0 Hz, roughly 100 K higher than traditional Snoe
